subject: Climate & Environment
title: Palm Oil and Tropical Forests
description: One-minute skill: Palm Oil and Tropical Forests.

hook.text: Palm oil is in half the products on supermarket shelves — from cookies to shampoo.

buildup.text: Oil palms produce more oil per hectare than any other crop. That makes them very profitable.

discovery.text: Indonesia and Malaysia produce 85% of the world's palm oil — mostly on former rainforest.

twist.text: Certified sustainable palm oil exists, but it accounts for less than 20% of global supply.

climax.text: Boycotting palm oil entirely could backfire — alternatives need even more land to produce.

punchline.text: The issue isn't the palm. It's where we plant it.

quiz.question: Why is palm oil so widely used?
options: It yields more oil per hectare than any other crop

details.summary: Palm oil is the world's most consumed vegetable oil, found in roughly half of all supermarket products. Its production has driven massive deforestation in Indonesia and Malaysia, destroying orangutan habitat and draining carbon-rich peatlands.
details.whyItMatters: Palm oil connects everyday consumer products to tropical destruction. Demand is growing, making sustainable sourcing and enforcement critical.
takeaways: Palm oil is in about 50 percent of packaged consumer products
Indonesia and Malaysia produce over 85 percent of global supply
Oil palm plantations have replaced millions of hectares of rainforest

faq.question: Is boycotting palm oil the solution?
faq.answer: Boycotts can backfire because palm oil is the most land-efficient oilseed. Replacing it with soy, sunflower, or rapeseed would require more land overall. Supporting certified sustainable palm oil and pressing for enforcement is more effective.

faq.question: What does certified sustainable palm oil mean?
faq.answer: RSPO certification prohibits clearing primary forest and peat after 2005, requires social safeguards, and mandates environmental management. However, only about 19 percent of global palm oil is certified, and enforcement remains inconsistent.
